explication:
aria2 is a C++11 command-line downloader with a library mode. The main deliverable is `src/aria2c`; a separate `libaria2` API is exposed from `src/aria2api.cc` and headers under `src/includes/aria2`. The codebase is organized as a single core engine with protocol-specific subsystems plugged into it.

The top-level control flow starts in `src/main.cc`, which parses options, constructs the download/session context, and drives the `DownloadEngine`. `OptionParser`, `OptionHandler`, `prefs`, and related classes form the configuration boundary between user input, config files, and runtime behavior.

The central runtime model is request-group based. A `RequestGroup` represents one download job and is managed by `RequestGroupMan`; each group is split into requests, segments, and pieces depending on protocol and file type. This is where aria2’s segmented downloading, mirror selection, and bandwidth-aware scheduling converge.

Protocol handling is split into dedicated subsystems rather than one monolith. HTTP, FTP, and SFTP each have their own connection/download command classes, request/response types, and negotiation flows. These components sit on top of a shared socket and event-poll layer, so protocol logic stays separate from transport and scheduling.

BitTorrent is a large subsystem of its own. It includes peer connection/state management, message factories/dispatchers/validators, tracker interaction, DHT, PEX, metadata exchange, and piece selection strategies. The BitTorrent code shares the same engine-level scheduling and disk-writing infrastructure, but has its own swarm-centric control plane and persistent state.

Metalink support is another major front-end to the core engine. The Metalink parser and request-group builder translate Metalink documents into one or more download groups, then feed them into the same downloader pipeline. Metalink-specific post-download handlers add checksum validation, signature handling, and mirror/priority logic.

Integrity and content verification are first-class boundaries in the architecture. The repo has separate checksum, chunk-checksum, hash, and validator abstractions, plus protocol-aware validators for torrent pieces and Metalink chunks. This means verification is not bolted on after download; it is integrated into the data flow while bytes are being written.

The storage layer is abstracted behind disk writer/adaptor interfaces. There are implementations for direct writes, buffered writes, byte-array/JSON/bencode/XML-RPC writers, multi-file and single-file allocation strategies, and write caches. This boundary isolates protocol logic from filesystem layout, preallocation, resume data, and partial-file handling.

Networking and concurrency are handled through a portable event model. The repo contains multiple event-poll backends (`epoll`, `kqueue`, `poll`, `select`, `libuv`) and socket/connection abstractions that hide platform differences. DNS resolution, proxy handling, and async connect flows sit on this transport foundation.

The daemon and remote-control surface is built into the same process. aria2 exposes JSON-RPC over HTTP and WebSocket, plus XML-RPC, through dedicated HTTP server, RPC method, request/response, and WebSocket session classes. The bundled `deps/wslay` subtree provides the WebSocket framing implementation used by this control plane.

Persistence is explicit and protocol-specific. aria2 can serialize session state, store BitTorrent DHT routing tables, save cookies, and preserve download metadata/progress info. Those artifacts are used to resume downloads, reconnect to swarms, and maintain identity/state across runs.

Platform-specific crypto and TLS are selected behind abstraction layers. The tree includes OpenSSL, GnuTLS, Apple TLS, and Windows TLS implementations, plus multiple message-digest and key-exchange backends. Which implementation is active depends on build configuration and available libraries, so the diagram should show a pluggable security boundary rather than a fixed dependency.

The repository also carries substantial build and distribution infrastructure. Autotools (`configure.ac`, `Makefile.am`, `m4`) drives the native build, with dedicated Dockerfiles and config wrappers for Android, MinGW/Windows, Raspberry Pi, and macOS packaging. Tests under `test/` are extensive and map closely to the core subsystems, while `doc/` contains the Sphinx-based manuals and RPC/XML-RPC docs.
